subject: SLO measurement methodology, alerting, and customer metric access - procurement questions
messages:
From: Jeffrey Lopez <jeffrey.lopez@nimblehealth.com>
To: Rachel Kim <rachel_kim@redwood.ai>
Cc: procurement@nimblehealth.com
Date: Tue, 12 May 2026 09:14:00 -0700
Subject: Procurement: specifics on uptime/latency measurement and customer dashboards

Hi Rachel —

Thanks for the quick intro call earlier. Procurement at NimbleHealth needs a short, concrete write-up for our legal and SRE teams describing exactly how Redwood measures SLOs for hosted customers. Specifically we need answers to:

1) What exact signal is used to calculate uptime (synthetic checks, successful requests, or user-facing success rate)? How are transient client/network failures treated?
2) How are latency SLOs defined (p50/p95/p99, which route level are they measured at)? What aggregation window and bucket size is used?
3) Do you provide customer-facing dashboards or a read-only metrics feed? If so, what is the retention window and are there role-based access controls?
4) How do maintenance windows and scheduled upgrades get excluded from SLO calculations? Can we request temporary carve-outs?
5) In an incident where regional capacity is exhausted and you fall back to a lower-tier model, how is that accounted for in SLA crediting?
6) Any clock-sync or time-zone assumptions that affect rolling-window computations?

If you can provide a short description and any attachments (sample dashboard invite, a measurement worksheet) that would be perfect — our deadline is EOD Friday for the procurement packet.

Appreciate it,
Jeff
Jeffrey Lopez
Procurement Lead, NimbleHealth

From: Rachel Kim <rachel_kim@redwood.ai>
To: Jeffrey Lopez <jeffrey.lopez@nimblehealth.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>, Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.ai>
Date: Tue, 12 May 2026 11:03:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Procurement: specifics on uptime/latency measurement and customer dashboards

Hi Jeff —

Thanks — good list. Looping in Marissa (Solutions) and Ben (SRE liaison); they can add the measurement specifics and sample artifacts. High level answers below so procurement has something while we pull the workbook:

- Signal: We compute uptime primarily from successful inference request observations at the model-route level (i.e., 2xx token-generation completions). Synthetic health checks are used for service-level guardrails and alerting, but they are not the sole basis for uptime SLOs. Client-network failures that fail before hitting our load balancer are excluded; failures after the LB are treated as failed requests.

- Latency: We publish p50/p95/p99 at the API route and model-variant level. Aggregation is over 1-minute buckets, rolled up to a rolling 30-day window by default (we can provide alternate windows in contracts).

- Dashboards: We offer a read-only Grafana dashboard per-account (regional scopes) and a metrics export endpoint for enterprises. Retention on the read-only dashboard is 90 days by default; richer telemetry exports (raw metrics) can be retained per contract. RBAC applies — admin vs read-only views.

- Maintenance & exceptions: Scheduled maintenance windows are excluded when requested in advance (we map them to a maintenance window that is excluded from the rolling window calculation). Short-term carve-outs (e.g., planned data plane migrations) are supported via a written exception request and will be applied retroactively where validated.

- Failover to lower-tier model: We track the active model variant serving each request. If we fail over to a compatible but lower-capacity/quality variant due to capacity constraints, those requests are still counted as successful requests for uptime but may be treated differently for a quality SLA; for billing or crediting we have explicit fallback policies captured in the contract.

- Time windows: All rolling windows are computed in UTC. Timestamps are normalized at the point of ingress using NTP-synced service clocks.

I'll attach the measurement workbook and a sample Grafana invite. Marissa/Ben — can you add any operational definitions (e.g., what constitutes a request failure vs a network pre-LB drop) and confirm the retention/export options?

Best,
Rachel Kim
Enterprise Sales, Redwood Inference

From: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>

Date: Wed, 13 May 2026 08:27:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Procurement: specifics on uptime/latency measurement and customer dashboards

Hi Jeff —

Adding a few operational clarifications from the SRE/telemetry side. I'm keeping this concise for procurement:

- Measurement unit: "successful inference request" means the service returned an OK response containing model output and full token stream (for streaming routes, a client-visible error mid-stream is treated as a failure). Internal retries that succeed before sending a response to the client are considered part of our server-side handling and the final observed outcome is used.

- Bucketization & rollup: We compute 1-minute histograms for latency and success counts. Those are stored in TSDB with 1m resolution; p95/p99 are computed from histogram envelopes and then rolled up to hourly/30-day rollups for SLO windows. The 1-minute buckets reduce noise from bursty traffic and are the basis of alerting.

- Synthetic vs real traffic: Synthetic probes run from multiple regions to monitor regional reachability and as an early warning. For contractual SLOs we use production traffic only (with clear definitions around bot traffic deduplication).

- Maintenance: To request exclusion, customers submit a maintenance notice at least 48 hours in advance via the console or support ticket. Emergency maintenance can be excluded with post-hoc validation (root cause + timeline) and a retroactive exception request.

- Regional fallbacks and crediting: If we proactively migrate traffic to a different region or model variant as part of graceful degradation, we annotate those request traces. Credits are determined per the contract: we default to counting only requests that returned 2xx as "available" but provide separate quality metrics that may influence credits if a lower-tier model materially changes output quality.

- Access & exports: Grafana invite = read-only by default (no query-writing). We can stream metrics to a customer-managed GCP/AWS account or provide scheduled raw-metrics exports (JSON/Prometheus) on a separate retention tier.

Attachments included: SLO-measurement-workbook.xlsx (worksheet with definitions and sample calculations), grafana-invite-template.txt (sample invite email).

If you need a one-page statement for legal that mirrors these operational definitions, I can produce it today.

Thanks,
Marissa Cole
Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

A short summary for your legal team is below — feel free to copy verbatim into procurement docs.

Short statement for procurement/legal (copyable):
Redwood Inference measures Service Level Objectives (SLOs) for hosted customers based on successful inference request observations at the API route and model-variant level. Latency SLOs (p50/p95/p99) are computed from 1-minute histogram buckets and evaluated over a rolling 30-day window in UTC. Scheduled maintenance windows submitted at least 48 hours in advance are excluded from SLO computations; emergency exclusions are handled via an exception request and validated post-event. Customer-facing, read-only Grafana dashboards (90-day retention) are provided by default; extended telemetry exports and custom retention are available under contract. Rolling-window computations use NTP-synced service clocks; timestamps are normalized at ingress.

Next steps:
- Please confirm if the 30-day rolling window is acceptable or if NimbleHealth needs a 90-day contractual window.
- If you want Grafana access now, reply with the list of emails for read-only invites and we'll provision them.

Thanks again — we can also set a short 30-min technical handoff between your SRE and our SREs next week if you'd like to walk through the workbook values.

Best,
